title: Twelve Vertices, Two Colours
statement: Each of the $12$ vertices of a regular $12$-sided polygon is coloured red or blue. In how many of the $2^{12}$ colourings is there no set of four vertices of the same colour that are the corners of a rectangle (a square counts as a rectangle), and no set of three vertices of the same colour that are the corners of an equilateral triangle?
hints: Number the vertices $0, 1, \dots, 11$ in order. Describe, in terms of these numbers, which four vertices form a rectangle and which three form an equilateral triangle.

The rectangles are the pairs of diameters $\{i, i + 6\}$, and the triangles are $\{i, i + 4, i + 8\}$. Use the Chinese remainder theorem: put vertex $i$ in row $i \bmod 4$ and column $i \bmod 3$ of a $4 \times 3$ array, and see what the triangles and the diameters become.

The triangles are the rows, and the diameters are the columns of two $2 \times 3$ blocks, one made of rows $0$ and $2$ and one of rows $1$ and $3$. No row may be one colour, and at most one diameter may be all red and at most one all blue. Sort the colourings of a block by its numbers of all-red and all-blue columns, then combine the two blocks.
solution:
Number the vertices $0, 1, \dots, 11$. A rectangle inscribed in a circle has diameters as diagonals, so the rectangles are the unions of two of the six diameters $\{i, i + 6\}$. The equilateral triangles are $\{i, i + 4, i + 8\}$. So a colouring is allowed when no triangle is one colour and at most one diameter is all red and at most one is all blue.

By the Chinese remainder theorem, put vertex $i$ in row $i \bmod 4$ and column $i \bmod 3$ of a $4 \times 3$ array. The triangles are the rows. Since $i + 6 \equiv i + 2 \pmod 4$ and $i + 6 \equiv i \pmod 3$, the diameters are the columns of the block of rows $0, 2$ and of the block of rows $1, 3$.

In one block each row is one of the $6$ rows that are not one colour. Let $(p, q)$ count its all-red and all-blue columns. Two equal rows with one red cell give $(1, 2)$, and two such rows that differ give $(0, 1)$. A row with one red cell and a row with two give $(1, 1)$ if the red cells overlap and $(0, 0)$ if not. Two equal rows with two red cells give $(2, 1)$, and two that differ give $(1, 0)$. So the usable blocks are $6$ of type $(0, 0)$, $6$ of type $(0, 1)$, $6$ of type $(1, 0)$ and $12$ of type $(1, 1)$.

The two blocks may not together have two all-red or two all-blue columns. This allows $(0,0)$ with $(0,0)$ in $36$ ways, $(0,0)$ with any other usable type in $2 \cdot 6 \cdot 24 = 288$ ways, and $(0,1)$ with $(1,0)$ in $2 \cdot 36 = 72$ ways. The total is $36 + 288 + 72 = 396$.
